title: Chapter 5: Length, perimeter, area and volume

questions.stem: A garden path is made from 8 paving stones, each \(45\text{ cm}\) long, laid end to end. What is the total length of the path in metres?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of stones by the length of each, then convert to metres.

steps.explain: Multiply the number of stones by the length of one stone.
Convert centimetres to metres by dividing by 100.

questions.stem: Write the unit you would use to measure each of these items. Then write the name of the measuring instrument you would use to make the measurement. The length of the playground
options: millimetres, measured with a trundle wheel
metres, measured with a tape measure or a trundle wheel
centimetres, measured with a tape measure or a trundle wheel
questions.hint: Estimate the length first, then pick the unit that gives a sensible number.

steps.explain: First estimate how long the length of the playground is. Think about the size of the object.
A playground is tens of metres long. Centimetres and millimetres are too small, kilometres too big. A trundle wheel or a long tape measure measures metres.
Pick the unit that gives a sensible, easy-to-say number: metres. Then choose the instrument that measures that unit well: a tape measure or a trundle wheel.
Why the other answers are wrong: they use a unit that is far too small (a huge number) or far too big (a tiny decimal), or an instrument that cannot measure this length.

keyPoints.note: Use the same units before you add or compare lengths.

steps.explain: First estimate how long the length of your shoe is. Think about the size of the object.
A shoe is about 25 cm long. Centimetres (or millimetres) are best and a ruler is the right instrument.
Pick the unit that gives a sensible, easy-to-say number: centimetres. Then choose the instrument that measures that unit well: a ruler.
Why the other answers are wrong: they use a unit that is far too small (a huge number) or far too big (a tiny decimal), or an instrument that cannot measure this length.

questions.stem: Jenny cut a 70-centimetre piece of string from a length of 10 metres. How much string was left?
questions.hint: Use the same unit for both lengths before you subtract.

steps.explain: The two lengths are in different units, so change them to the same unit first. \(10 \ \text{m} = 1000 \ \text{cm}\) (multiply by 100).
Subtract the piece she cut: 1000 cm − 70 cm.
Change back to metres (divide by 100): \(930 \ \text{cm} = 9.3 \ \text{m}\).
Check: \(9.3 \ \text{m} + 0.7 \ \text{m} = 10 \ \text{m}\). ✓

Why the other answers are wrong: one uses the wrong operation, one leaves out a step, and one has a slip in the decimal point or a unit mix-up (for example adding metres and centimetres without converting).

keyPoints.note: Find the quantity asked for: add, subtract, multiply or divide.
Use the same units before you add or compare lengths.

Change to metres: divide by 100.

questions.stem: A miniature microchip sensor has a width of \\(3\\text{ cm}\) and \\(2\\text{ mm}\\). Express this width in centimetres as a decimal.
questions.hint: Recall that \\(10\\text{ mm} = 1\\text{ cm}\\). Convert the millimetres to centimetres first, then add it to the whole centimetre value.

steps.explain: Identify the measurement components and the conversion factor. The width is \\(3\\text{ cm}\) and \\(2\\text{ mm}\\), and we know that \\(10\\text{ mm} = 1\\text{ cm}\\).
Convert the \\(2\\text{ mm}\) component into centimetres by dividing by \\(10\\). This shifts the digit one place value down.
Add the converted centimetre decimal to the original \\(3\\text{ cm}\) to get the final total length.
Conclude that the decimal equivalent of the width is 3.2 cm.

steps.explain: Identify the measurements and the conversion factor. The length is \\(4\\text{ m}\) and \\(6\\text{ cm}\\), and we know that \\(100\\text{ cm} = 1\\text{ m}\\).

Add the converted metre value to the original \\(4\\text{ m}\) length.
Conclude that the mounting rail length expressed as a decimal is 4.06 metres.

steps.explain: Decide which way to convert. We change centimetres into metres. metres are the bigger unit  so there will be FEWER of them: divide by 100.

steps.explain: Decide which way to convert. We change metres into kilometres. kilometres are the bigger unit  so there will be FEWER of them: divide by 1 000.

questions.stem: Martin bought two pieces of wood from the timber yard. One piece was 3 m 65 cm long. The other piece was 4 m 45 cm long. If both pieces of wood were placed end to end, what would their total length be?
questions.hint: Add metres to metres and centimetres to centimetres (carry over 100 cm into a metre).

steps.explain: Change each length to centimetres. \(3 \ \text{m} 65 \ \text{cm} = 300 \ \text{cm} + 65 \ \text{cm}\).
\(4 \ \text{m} 45 \ \text{cm} = 400 \ \text{cm} + 45 \ \text{cm}\).
Add the two lengths: \(365 + 445 = 810 \ \text{cm}\).
Change to metres (divide by 100): \(810 \ \text{cm} = 8.1 \ \text{m} = 8 \ \text{m} 10 \ \text{cm}\).
Check by adding the metres and the centimetres separately: \(3 + 4 = 7 \ \text{m}\) and \(65 + 45 = 110 \ \text{cm} = 1 \ \text{m} 10 \ \text{cm}\), so 8 m 10 cm. ✓

Why the other answers are wrong: one uses the wrong operation, one leaves out a step, and one has a slip in the decimal point or a unit mix-up (for example adding metres and centimetres without converting).

keyPoints.note: Total means add all the amounts.
Use the same units before you add or compare lengths.

steps.explain: Check: the shape fits in a box 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall. A plain rectangle that size has perimeter 2 × (2+3) = 10 cm; every notch adds extra length.
Why the other answers are wrong: they miss one of the short sides of the notches, or count the squares inside (the area) instead of the length around the edge.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter is the total length around the shape: add all the sides.

steps.explain: Check: the shape fits in a box 3 cm wide and 5 cm tall. A plain rectangle that size has perimeter 2 × (3+5) = 16 cm; every notch adds extra length.
Why the other answers are wrong: they miss one of the short sides of the notches, or count the squares inside (the area) instead of the length around the edge.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter is the total length around the shape: add all the sides.

steps.explain: Check: the shape fits in a box 6 cm wide and 5 cm tall. A plain rectangle that size has perimeter 2 × (6+5) = 22 cm; every notch adds extra length.
Why the other answers are wrong: they miss one of the short sides of the notches, or count the squares inside (the area) instead of the length around the edge.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter is the total length around the shape: add all the sides.

steps.explain: Check: the shape fits in a box 6 cm wide and 5 cm tall. A plain rectangle that size has perimeter 2 × (6+5) = 22 cm; every notch adds extra length.
Why the other answers are wrong: they miss one of the short sides of the notches, or count the squares inside (the area) instead of the length around the edge.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter is the total length around the shape: add all the sides.

steps.explain: Check: the shape fits in a box 5 cm wide and 5 cm tall. A plain rectangle that size has perimeter 2 × (5+5) = 20 cm; every notch adds extra length.
Why the other answers are wrong: they miss one of the short sides of the notches, or count the squares inside (the area) instead of the length around the edge.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter is the total length around the shape: add all the sides.

questions.stem: Use the length and width of the rectangle to calculate its perimeter. Length 8 cm, width 6 cm. What is the perimeter in cm?
questions.hint: Make the units the same, add the length and width, then double.

steps.explain: A rectangle has length 8 cm and width 6 cm. We need its perimeter in cm.
Add the length and the width.
Double the result (a rectangle has two lengths and two widths).
Why the other answers are wrong: adding length and width only once, multiplying (area), or adding mm to cm without converting.

questions.stem: Which is the correct area for each rectangle? Length \(3\ \text{m}\), width \(50\ \text{cm}\).
questions.hint: Make both measurements the same unit, multiply, and give the answer in square units.

steps.explain: The units are different (m and cm). Change 50 cm to metres: divide by 100.
Multiply in metres: \(3 \times  0.5 = 1.5\).

Another way: \(3 \ \text{m} = 300 \ \text{cm}\), and \(300 \times  50 = 15\,000 \ \text{cm}^2\), which equals 1.5 m² (\(10\,000 \ \text{cm}^2 = 1 \ \text{m}^2\)). So 150 cm² and 15 m² are too small / too big.
Why the other answers are wrong: they add or double the sides, or they use the wrong units.

keyPoints.note: note
Area of a rectangle = length × width, in square units.

questions.stem: Which is the correct area for each rectangle? Length \(1.5\ \text{cm}\), width \(800\ \text{mm}\).
questions.hint: Make both measurements the same unit, multiply, and give the answer in square units.

steps.explain: The units are different (cm and mm). Change 800 mm to centimetres: divide by 10.
Multiply in centimetres: \(1.5 \times  80 = 120\) (\(1 \times  80 = 80\) and \(0.5 \times  80 = 40\)).
1200 mm² is too small (it would be 12 cm²); 81.5 adds the lengths.
Why the other answers are wrong: they add or double the sides, or they use the wrong units.

Area of a rectangle = length × width, in square units.

questions.stem: Which is the correct area for each rectangle? Length \(1250\ \text{mm}\), width \(30\ \text{cm}\).
questions.hint: Make both measurements the same unit, multiply, and give the answer in square units.

steps.explain: Change both to metres: \(1250 \ \text{mm} = 1.25 \ \text{m}\) (divide by 1000) and \(30 \ \text{cm} = 0.3 \ \text{m}\) (divide by 100).
Multiply: \(1.25 \times  0.3 = 0.375\) (\(125 \times  3 = 375\), then 3 decimal places).
1280 cm² adds 1250 + 30 (no multiplication); 37 500 is not in square metres (it is 1250 × 30 with no unit change).
Why the other answers are wrong: they add or double the sides, or they use the wrong units.

Why the other answers are wrong: one forgets a missing side (or uses a side twice), one counts the area when the perimeter is asked (or the reverse), and one has an addition slip.

keyPoints.note: Area of a rectangle = length × width, in square units.

steps.explain: Multiply 3 × 5 first, then halve it.
The answer as a mixed number: 7½ cm².
Both triangles you could draw have the same area, because the formula only needs the base and the height.
Why the other answers are wrong: 15 forgets the ½; 8 rounds up; 3 is only the base.

keyPoints.note: Area of a rectangle = length × width, in square units.
Area of a triangle = half × base × height.

questions.stem: Convert 250 000 square metres to hectares.
questions.hint: Divide by 10 000 (move the decimal point 4 places left). Hectares are bigger than square metres.

steps.explain: Decide which way to convert. We change square metres into hectares. hectares are the bigger unit  so there will be FEWER of them: divide by 10 000.
The relationship is \(1 \ \text{ha} = 10\,000 \ \text{m}^2\). To divide by 10 000 we move the decimal point 4 places to the left.
Move the decimal point 4 places to the left (write zeros if you run out of digits). If the answer is a whole number the decimal point is not needed.

questions.stem: A staircase is made from 1 cm³ cubes in 4 layers (the layers have 4 × 4, 4 × 3, 4 × 2 and 4 × 1 cubes). a How many cubes were used to make this staircase? b What is the volume of the staircase? c How many more centimetre cubes would you need to make a 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm cube?
options: a 44 cubes; b 44 cm³; c 20 more cubes
a 40 cubes; b 40 cm³; c 24 more cubes
a 40 cubes; b 40 cm³; c 64 more cubes
a 10 cubes; b 10 cm³; c 54 more cubes
questions.hint: Count the cubes in each layer and add; a full 4 × 4 × 4 cube has 64 cubes.

steps.explain: The staircase has 4 layers. Each layer is 4 cubes wide and gets shorter as we go up: 4 cubes long in layer 1, then 3, then 2, then 1.
Count the cubes in each layer.
Part a: add the layers to find the number of cubes.
Part b: each cube is 1 cm³, so the volume equals the number of cubes.
Part c: a 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm cube needs \(4 \times  4 \times  4 = 64\) cubes. We already have 40, so we need 64 − 40 more.
Why the other answers are wrong: 64 forgets to subtract the cubes already used; 10 adds only the numbers 4+3+2+1; 44 is a slip in the addition.

questions.stem: This rectangular prism has a volume of 120 cm³. Its height is 5 cm and its length is 6 cm. Find its width.
questions.hint: Divide the volume by the product of the two known measurements.

steps.explain: We know the volume and two of the three measurements. Volume = length × width × height, so to find the unknown one we DIVIDE the volume by the other two measurements.
The other two measurements are length = 6 cm and height = 5 cm. Multiply them first.
Divide the volume 120 cm³ by 30.
Check by multiplying all three measurements: the volume must come back.
So the width is 4 cm.
Why the other answers are wrong: subtracting, dividing by only one measurement, or multiplying instead of dividing.

steps.explain: So prism B has 24 cubes and its volume is 24 cm³.
Why the other answers are wrong: counting only one layer, adding the measurements, or a slip of a few cubes.

keyPoints.note: Volume of a prism = length × width × height, in cubic units.
Volume of a cube = side × side × side.
Work out what is being counted, then choose the operation.

questions.stem: Juliet collects small rectangular boxes that measure 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm. How many of these small boxes would fit inside a larger box that measures 60 cm × 30 cm × 24 cm?
questions.hint: Count how many small boxes fit along each edge, then multiply (or divide the volumes).

steps.explain: Compare the sizes. The small box is 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm and the big box is 60 cm × 30 cm × 24 cm. Count how many small boxes fit along each edge of the big box.
Along the 60 cm edge: \(60 \div  4 = 15\) boxes.
Along the 30 cm edge: \(30 \div  3 = 10\) boxes.
Along the 24 cm edge: \(24 \div  2 = 12\) boxes.
Multiply the three numbers: boxes in one layer = \(15 \times  10 = 150\), and there are 12 layers.
Check with volumes: big box \(60 \times  30 \times  24 = 43\,200 \ \text{cm}^3\); small box \(4 \times  3 \times  2 = 24 \ \text{cm}^3\); \(43\,200 \div  24 = 1800\). ✓
Why the other answers are wrong: 43 200 is the volume of the big box (not the number of boxes); 37 adds the counts; the others are slips.

questions.stem: The Terrific Tea Company imported a box of tea that was 12 cm long and 8 cm wide. After drinking one-third of the tea, there was still 576 cm³ of tea left in the box. Calculate the height of the box.
questions.hint: Two-thirds of the volume is 576. Find the full volume first, then divide by length × width.

steps.explain: After drinking one-third of the tea, two-thirds are left. The 576 cm³ left is therefore 2 of 3 equal parts.
Find one third: \(576 \div  2 = 288 \ \text{cm}^3\).
The box was full, which is 3 thirds: 3 × 288.
Height of the box = volume ÷ (length × width) = 864 ÷ (12 × 8).
Check: \(12 \times  8 \times  9 = 864\) and two-thirds of 864 is 576. ✓
Why the other answers are wrong: 6 uses the 576 as the full volume (\(576 \div  96 = 6\)); the others are slips.

questions.stem: Tara built a cube with side length 7 cm. How many more centimetre cubes does she need to make a cube with side length 8 cm?

questions.stem: Rosie's shed measures 3 m × 8 m. When it rains, 4 mm of rain falls on the shed roof each hour. What is the total amount of water collected in 3 hours?
questions.hint: Volume = area of the roof × depth of rain (in metres); then \(1 \ \text{m}^3 = 1000 \ \text{L}\).

steps.explain: The shed roof is 3 m by 8 m. Rain falls evenly over the roof, so the water collected is a flat box of water as big as the roof and as deep as the rain.
In 3 hours the rain is \(4 \ \text{mm} \times  3 = 12 \ \text{mm}\) deep. Change millimetres to metres (divide by 1000) to match the roof measurements.
Volume of water = roof area × depth of rain.
\(1 \ \text{m}^3 = 1000\) litres, so multiply by 1000 to get litres.
Check: 4 mm of rain on 24 m² is \(24 \times  0.004 = 0.096 \ \text{m}^3 = 96 \ \text{L}\) each hour.
Why the other answers are wrong: leaving the answer in m³ (not litres), or a slip in the mm → m conversion.

keyPoints.note: Total means add all the amounts.

questions.stem: Sharon bought a rectangular water tank measuring 8 m × 9 m × 300 mm. How many litres of water can Sharon's tank hold?
questions.hint: Change 300 mm to metres, find the volume in m³, then multiply by 1000.

steps.explain: The tank is 8 m long, 9 m wide and 300 mm deep. Change 300 mm to metres (divide by 1000) so all the measurements are in metres.
Volume = length × width × height.
1 m³ holds 1000 litres, so multiply by 1000.
Check: 21.6 m³ is 21.6 kilolitres, which is 21 600 L. ✓
Why the other answers are wrong: 21.6 is in cubic metres (not litres); the others have the wrong power of 10.

keyPoints.note: Work out what is being counted, then choose the operation.

questions.stem: Sharon collects water from a roof measuring 6 m × 2 m. If rain falls at 5 mm per hour, how long will it take to fill her tank? (The tank holds 21 600 litres.)
questions.hint: Find the litres collected each hour, then divide the tank's capacity by that.

steps.explain: The roof is 6 m by 2 m. Its area is 12 m².
5 mm of rain is 0.005 m. Water collected each hour = roof area × depth.
Change to litres: \(1 \ \text{m}^3 = 1000 \ \text{L}\).
The tank holds 21 600 L (from part a). Divide by the water collected each hour.
Check: \(60 \times  360 = 21\,600\). ✓ That is 15 days of non-stop rain.
Why the other answers are wrong: 36 and 3600 have a power of 10 slip; 4320 uses the wrong amount per hour.

questions.stem: A skipping rope is 5.83 metres long. How many skipping ropes can be made from a rope of length 55 metres?
questions.hint: Divide 55 by 5.83 and look for the largest whole number that fits.

steps.explain: Divide the total rope by the length of one skipping rope.
Try whole numbers: \(5.83 \times  9 = 52.47\) (\(5 \times  9 = 45\) and \(0.83 \times  9 = 7.47\)), and \(5.83 \times  10 = 58.3\) is more than 55.
So 9 whole ropes can be made.
What is left over: \(55 - 52.47 = 2.53\) metres.

Why the other answers are wrong: one uses the wrong operation, one leaves out a step, and one has a slip in the decimal point or a unit mix-up (for example adding metres and centimetres without converting).

keyPoints.note: Work out what is being counted, then choose the operation.
Use the same units before you add or compare lengths.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 5: Length, perimeter, area and volume

questions.stem: Convert this measurement to hectares. If your answer is not a whole number, write it as a decimal. 10 000 m²
questions.hint: Divide by 10 000 (move the decimal point 4 places left). Hectares are bigger than square metres.

steps.explain: Decide which way to convert. We change square metres into hectares. hectares are the bigger unit  so there will be FEWER of them: divide by 10 000.
The relationship is \(1 \ \text{ha} = 10\,000 \ \text{m}^2\). To divide by 10 000 we move the decimal point 4 places to the left.
Move the decimal point 4 places to the left (write zeros if you run out of digits). If the answer is a whole number the decimal point is not needed.

questions.stem: Each sheep on Mr B. A. Lamb's farm requires 15 m² of grass. How many sheep can Mr Lamb put in a paddock of 1 hectare?
questions.hint: Change the area to m², then divide by 15.

steps.explain: Each sheep needs 15 m² of grass. The number of sheep = the area of the paddock ÷ 15 m² (both in square metres).
Change the area to square metres: 1 hectare = 10000 m² (1 hectare = 10 000 m²).
Divide: \(10000 \div  15 = 666\) remainder 10.
A paddock cannot hold part of a sheep, so we use the whole number of sheep. The 10 m² left over is not enough for another sheep.
Check: sheep × 15 m² must not be more than the area.
Why the other answers are wrong: dividing hectares by 15 without changing to m², rounding up (a part-sheep does not fit), or a slip in the division.

keyPoints.note: 1 hectare = 10 000 square metres.

questions.stem: Convert this measurement in litres to millilitres by multiplying by 1000. 4 litres
questions.hint: Multiply by 1 000 (move the decimal point 3 places right). Millilitres are smaller than litres.

steps.explain: Decide which way to convert. We change litres into millilitres. millilitres are the smaller unit  so there will be MORE of them: multiply by 1 000.
The relationship is \(1 \ \text{L} = 1000 \ \text{mL}\). To multiply by 1 000 we move the decimal point 3 places to the right.
Move the decimal point 3 places to the right (write zeros if you run out of digits).

steps.explain: So 4 L = 4000 mL.
